title: How to Win Friends and Influence People
author: Dale Carnegie
summary:
First published in 1936, Dale Carnegie's How to Win Friends and Influence People distills decades of his public-speaking and interpersonal-skills courses into a set of concrete, repeatable habits for getting along with — and appropriately influencing — other people. The book rests on one foundational premise: people are driven above all by a deep craving to feel important, appreciated, and understood, and nearly every technique Carnegie teaches is a different, honest application of that insight rather than a manipulation around it. The book is organized into four parts, each built from a numbered list of specific principles rather than abstract theory, and each principle is illustrated with a real anecdote — Theodore Roosevelt, Abraham Lincoln, Charles Schwab, John Wanamaker, and ordinary students from Carnegie's own courses — so the reader experiences the ideas as tested habits with observable results, not platitudes.

Carnegie opens with what he calls the fundamental techniques in handling people: don't criticize, condemn, or complain, because criticism puts people on the defensive and rarely produces the change you actually want, while quietly building resentment; give honest and sincere appreciation, sharply distinguished from flattery, which people see through and distrust; and arouse in the other person an eager want by framing requests around the other person's interest, not just your own. From there the book turns to six ways to make people like you — becoming genuinely interested in others, smiling, remembering and using a person's name, listening well and encouraging others to talk about themselves, talking in terms of the other person's interests, and making people feel sincerely important — all variations on the idea that attention and appreciation, given without an angle, are the most reliable way to earn someone's goodwill.

The book's third section addresses how to win people to your way of thinking without triggering the defensiveness that direct persuasion usually causes: avoid arguments entirely, since even a technical win in an argument tends to lose the relationship; show real respect for the other person's opinions; admit your own mistakes quickly and emphatically; start any disagreement in a friendly way; get early agreement on small points before raising the harder ones; let the other person feel that an idea is theirs; and appeal to nobler motives rather than self-interest alone. The final section applies the same philosophy to leadership and correction — how to change someone's behavior without arousing resentment — through techniques like beginning with genuine praise, calling attention to mistakes indirectly, talking about your own errors before criticizing someone else's, asking questions instead of giving orders, letting the other person save face, and praising every improvement, however small, so the person has a reputation worth living up to.

What holds the whole book together is less a formula than a stance: that lasting influence over people comes from treating them as the emotionally invested, self-interested, pride-driven beings they actually are, and choosing patience, appreciation, and tact over criticism, argument, and command. Carnegie never claims these techniques are effortless — several chapters acknowledge how unnatural it feels to praise someone you're frustrated with, or to let a disagreement go unwon — but he presents them as skills anyone can build through deliberate practice, the same way his courses trained thousands of readers to speak in public. Despite its age, the book endures because its central claim has held up: most of what determines whether people cooperate with you is not the logic of your argument but whether they feel respected, heard, and important in the exchange.

sections.title: Fundamental Techniques in Handling People
sections.summary:
This opening section lays the groundwork the rest of the book depends on: before covering any specific tactic for winning someone over, Carnegie wants to establish the basic emotional reality he thinks most people get wrong when dealing with others — that human beings are not persuaded by logic alone, and that the person you're dealing with cares more about their own pride and sense of importance than about being right.

The section's substance is three tightly linked principles. The first, don't criticize, condemn, or complain, argues that direct criticism almost never produces the change you're hoping for — it puts the other person on the defensive, wounds their pride, and breeds resentment that outlasts whatever behavior prompted the criticism, and Carnegie backs this with historical examples showing that even highly capable, successful people default to criticism and pay for it in damaged relationships. The second, give honest and sincere appreciation, draws a hard line between appreciation and flattery: flattery is insincere and self-serving, and people usually see through it, while genuine appreciation focuses on specific, deserved recognition of another person's value, and Carnegie treats the craving to be appreciated as one of the deepest, most universal human needs. The third, arouse in the other person an eager want, reframes persuasion itself — instead of pushing what you want the other person to do, find and speak to what they already want, since people act on their own desires far more reliably than on someone else's.

The section closes by presenting these three principles not as isolated tips but as the operating system for everything that follows: every later technique in the book — making people like you, winning them to your way of thinking, leading without giving offense — is, at bottom, a specific application of withholding criticism, giving real appreciation, and speaking to the other person's wants rather than your own.
keyLessons: Criticism rarely changes behavior — it puts people on the defensive and creates resentment that outlasts whatever prompted it.
Draw a hard line between appreciation and flattery: appreciation is specific and sincere, flattery is self-serving and usually obvious.
Frame what you want in terms of what the other person already wants; people act far more reliably on their own desires than on yours.

sections.title: Six Ways to Make People Like You
sections.summary:
Having established the underlying philosophy, this section turns to concrete, repeatable behaviors anyone can practice to become more likable — not through charisma or luck, but through a small set of habits Carnegie argues are available to everyone regardless of personality.

The section works through six specific habits. Becoming genuinely interested in other people comes first and underlies the rest — Carnegie argues you can learn more about someone, and earn more goodwill, in two months of real curiosity about them than in two years of trying to make them curious about you. Smiling and using a person's name follow as small but disproportionately powerful signals — Carnegie calls a person's name the sweetest and most important sound they'll ever hear, because it confirms they've been noticed as an individual rather than processed as a generic interaction. Being a good listener and encouraging others to talk about themselves works because most people are, by Carnegie's account, far more interested in their own concerns than in someone else's, so genuine listening reliably outperforms trying to be interesting. The final two habits — talking in terms of the other person's interests and making them feel important through sincere, specific recognition — tie back directly to the appreciation principle from section one, applied now to the specific goal of being liked rather than just respected.

The section resolves by noting that none of these six habits require unusual talent or charm — they require attention, redirected away from yourself and toward the other person, which is exactly why Carnegie treats them as learnable skills rather than personality traits, and why they set up the harder persuasion work of the next section.
keyLessons: Genuine curiosity about other people builds more goodwill faster than trying to make yourself interesting to them.
Small signals — a smile, using someone's name, remembering details about them — carry disproportionate weight because they signal individual attention.
People are far more invested in their own concerns than in yours; being a good listener consistently outperforms being a good talker.

sections.title: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
sections.summary:
This section tackles the hardest persuasion problem in the book: how to actually change someone's mind or get their agreement without triggering the defensiveness that direct argument reliably produces. Carnegie treats this as the section where the book's underlying philosophy gets tested against real disagreement, not just pleasant interaction.

The chapter opens by ruling out arguing altogether — Carnegie's position is that you effectively can't win an argument, because losing it costs you the point and winning it typically costs you the relationship, so the only reliable path is avoiding the argument structure in the first place. From there it builds a sequence of techniques for getting agreement without confrontation: show genuine respect for the other person's opinions even when you disagree, admit your own mistakes quickly and emphatically before pointing out theirs, and begin any difficult conversation in a friendly, non-adversarial way rather than opening with the disagreement itself. Carnegie also recommends deliberately securing early agreement on small, easy points — getting the other person saying "yes, yes" — before introducing the harder ask, on the theory that momentum toward agreement is easier to sustain than reversing an early "no." The section's more advanced techniques include letting the other person feel that an idea originated with them, since people defend and commit to ideas they believe they came up with far more than ideas handed to them, genuinely trying to see the situation from the other person's point of view before arguing your own, and appealing to nobler motives — framing a request in terms of fairness, honor, or principle rather than only self-interest.

By the end of the section, Carnegie has replaced "winning" as the goal of disagreement with something closer to alignment: getting the other person to arrive, on their own terms and with their own sense of ownership, at the conclusion you were hoping for. That reframe sets up the book's final section, which applies the same non-confrontational logic specifically to correcting behavior and leading others.
keyLessons: Treat arguments as unwinnable by design — even a technical victory usually costs you the other person's goodwill.
Secure small, easy agreements early in a conversation; momentum toward "yes" is easier to build on than reversing an early "no."
People commit far more strongly to ideas they believe they originated themselves than to ideas presented to them directly.
Genuinely understanding the other person's point of view before arguing your own makes persuasion far more effective than restating your position louder.

sections.title: Be a Leader — How to Change People Without Giving Offense or Arousing Resentment
sections.summary:
The book's final section narrows to a specific and harder version of influence: how to actually change someone's behavior — as a manager, parent, or leader — without provoking the resentment that direct correction usually causes. Carnegie treats this as leadership's central technical problem, distinct from simply being liked or winning agreement in conversation.

The chapter supplies a sequence of techniques designed to make correction feel supportive rather than punitive. Beginning with honest praise before raising a problem softens the ground for the criticism that follows, and calling attention to mistakes indirectly — through suggestion or question rather than blunt statement — lets the other person reach the correction themselves instead of having it imposed. Talking about your own mistakes before criticizing someone else's levels the emotional field, and asking questions instead of giving direct orders preserves the other person's sense of autonomy, which Carnegie treats as essential to getting willing cooperation rather than resentful compliance. He also emphasizes letting the other person save face even when they're clearly at fault, praising every improvement no matter how small to keep motivation moving in the right direction, and giving people a reputation to live up to — deliberately treating a trait you want to encourage as though the person already reliably displays it, which tends to make them grow into it.

The section, and the book, close by tying leadership back to the very first principle Carnegie introduced: that people respond to how they're made to feel far more than to the technical correctness of what they're told. A leader who can correct behavior while preserving someone's pride and sense of importance gets lasting, willing change; a leader who relies on direct criticism gets compliance at best and quiet resentment at worst.
keyLessons: Open corrective conversations with genuine praise before raising the problem — it changes how the criticism that follows is received.
Ask questions instead of giving direct orders when you want someone to change; it preserves their sense of autonomy and ownership.
Let people save face and praise every improvement, however small, to keep them moving toward the change you want.
Give someone a reputation to live up to — treating a desired trait as though it's already theirs tends to make them grow into it.
Never criticize, condemn, or complain about people directly — it puts them on the defensive and rarely produces real change.
Give honest, specific appreciation rather than vague flattery, which people can usually tell apart from sincerity.
Become genuinely interested in the other person before expecting them to be interested in you.
You can't win an argument in any way that matters — even a technical win usually loses the relationship.
Let the other person feel an idea is theirs; people commit far more to ideas they believe they originated.
When you need to correct someone, begin with genuine praise and talk about your own mistakes first before pointing out theirs.
Ask questions instead of giving direct orders when you want someone to change their behavior — it preserves their sense of autonomy.
Always let the other person save face, and praise every improvement, however small, to keep them moving in the right direction.

quotes.text: Any fool can criticize, complain, and condemn—and most fools do. But it takes character and self-control to be understanding and forgiving.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: Criticism is futile because it puts a person on the defensive and usually makes him strive to justify himself. Criticism is dangerous, because it wounds a person's precious pride, hurts his sense of importance, and arouses resentment.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: Instead of condemning people, let's try to understand them. Let's try to figure out why they do what they do. That's a lot more profitable and intriguing than criticism; and it breeds sympathy, tolerance and kindness.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: If some people are so hungry for a feeling of importance that they actually go insane to get it, imagine what miracle you and I can achieve by giving people honest appreciation this side of insanity.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: The deepest principle in human nature is the craving to be appreciated.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: Arouse in the other person an eager want. He who can do this has the whole world with him. He who cannot walks a lonely way.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: You can make more friends in two months by becoming interested in other people than you can in two years by trying to get other people interested in you.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: To be interesting, be interested.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: Remember that a person's name is to that person the sweetest and most important sound in any language.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: Actions speak louder than words, and a smile says, 'I like you. You make me happy. I am glad to see you.'
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: Talk to someone about themselves and they'll listen for hours.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: A person's toothache means more to that person than a famine in China which kills a million people. A boil on one's neck interests one more than forty earthquakes in Africa. Think of that the next time you start a conversation.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: You can't win an argument. You can't because if you lose it, you lose it; and if you win it, you lose it.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People
quotes.category: Winning People to Your Way of Thinking

quotes.text: I have come to the conclusion that there is only one way under high heaven to get the best of an argument—and that is to avoid it. Avoid it as you would avoid rattlesnakes and earthquakes.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People
quotes.category: Winning People to Your Way of Thinking

quotes.text: If you argue and rankle and contradict, you may achieve a victory sometimes; but it will be an empty victory because you will never get your opponent's good will.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People
quotes.category: Winning People to Your Way of Thinking

quotes.text: When dealing with people, remember you are not dealing with creatures of logic, but with creatures bristling with prejudice and motivated by pride and vanity.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People
quotes.category: Winning People to Your Way of Thinking

quotes.text: By fighting you never get enough, but by yielding you get more than you expected.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People
quotes.category: Winning People to Your Way of Thinking

quotes.text: If there is any one secret of success, it lies in the ability to get the other person's point of view and see things from that person's angle as well as from your own.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, quoting Henry Ford, in How to Win Friends and Influence People
quotes.category: Winning People to Your Way of Thinking

quotes.text: Buddha said: 'Hatred is never ended by hatred but by love,' and a misunderstanding is never ended by an argument but by tact, diplomacy, conciliation and a sympathetic desire to see the other person's viewpoint.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People
quotes.category: Winning People to Your Way of Thinking

quotes.text: Be 'hearty in your approbation and lavish in your praise,' and people will cherish your words and treasure them and repeat them over a lifetime – repeat them years after you have forgotten them.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: To change somebody's behavior, change the level of respect she receives by giving her a fine reputation to live up to. Act as though the trait you are trying to influence is already one of the person's outstanding characteristics.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: If you want to gather honey, don't kick over the beehive.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: Control your temper. Remember, you can measure the size of a person by what makes him or her angry.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: I learned thirty years ago that it is foolish to scold. I have enough trouble overcoming my own limitations without fretting over the fact that God has not seen fit to distribute evenly the gift of intelligence.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, quoting John Wanamaker, in How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: I consider my ability to arouse enthusiasm among my people the greatest asset I possess, and the way to develop the best that is in a person is by appreciation and encouragement. There is nothing else that so kills the ambitions of a person as criticisms from superiors. I never criticize anyone. I believe in giving a person incentive to work. So I am anxious to praise but loath to find fault.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, quoting Charles Schwab, in How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: It isn't what you have or who you are or where you are or what you are doing that makes you happy or unhappy. It is what you think about it.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: Don't be afraid of enemies who attack you. Be afraid of the friends who flatter you.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: Everybody in the world is seeking happiness—and there is one sure way to find it. That is by controlling your thoughts. Happiness doesn't depend on outward conditions. It depends on inner conditions.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: People who can put themselves in the place of other people, who can understand the workings of their minds, need never worry about what the future has in store for them.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.text: About 15 percent of one's financial success is due to one's technical knowledge and about 85 percent is due to skill in human engineering—to personality and the ability to lead people.
quotes.attribution: Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

authorBio.name: Dale Carnegie
authorBio.bio:
Dale Carnegie was born Dale Breckenridge Carnagey on November 24, 1888, on a farm near Maryville, Missouri, to a poor farming family; he later simplified the spelling of his surname to Carnegie, reportedly because people kept misspelling it. He grew up doing farm chores before dawn, attended a one-room schoolhouse, and discovered a talent and passion for public speaking through his high school debate team — an early interest that would define the rest of his life. He worked his way through what is now the University of Central Missouri, and after graduating spent several restless years in sales jobs, including selling correspondence courses and then bacon, soap, and lard for Armour and Company, before saving enough money to move to New York and chase an acting career, with little success.

The turning point came almost by accident. Working out of a YMCA in New York, Carnegie talked his way into teaching a public-speaking class in exchange for a share of the tuition fees, and when he ran out of prepared material on the first night, he improvised by asking students to speak about something that had genuinely made them angry — discovering that people spoke far more confidently and naturally about material they actually cared about. That course became wildly popular and evolved into what he eventually branded Dale Carnegie Training, an organization built around public speaking, salesmanship, and interpersonal skills that continues to operate internationally today. Carnegie spent years refining the material through the direct feedback of thousands of adult students, and in 1936 he distilled it into How to Win Friends and Influence People, which became an immediate bestseller and one of the best-selling nonfiction books ever published.

Carnegie continued writing and teaching for the rest of his life, publishing a biography of Abraham Lincoln and, in 1948, a companion volume on managing anxiety, How to Stop Worrying and Start Living, which became nearly as influential as his first book. He died of Hodgkin lymphoma in 1955, but the organization and philosophy he built outlived him by decades: Dale Carnegie Training is still run today, and his core insight — that lasting influence over other people comes from genuine attention and respect rather than argument or authority — remains one of the most widely cited ideas in popular self-help and business writing.
notableWorks: How to Stop Worrying and Start Living
The Quick and Easy Way to Effective Speaking
Public Speaking and Influencing Men in Business

whoThisIsFor: Anyone who deals with other people regularly — in business, leadership, sales, or personal relationships — and wants concrete, old-fashioned but well-tested habits for it.
whenToReadThis: A good re-read whenever a working relationship feels stuck or before a period of heavy negotiation, hiring, or team leadership.
sourceNotes: v2 retrofit. Whole-book summary, section summaries, section and book-level keyLessons, and authorBio.bio are original synthesis based on general knowledge of Carnegie's well-documented four-part structure and named principles; no book text was copied or paraphrased into those fields. All 30 quotes were sourced verbatim from Goodreads' work-quotes page for How to Win Friends and Influence People (goodreads.com/work/quotes/2370171), selected from the highest-liked, most-cited entries (thousands of likes each) to confirm genuine notability rather than obscurity. Several quotes are lines Carnegie himself quotes from others within his own text (Henry Ford, Charles Schwab, John Wanamaker, Buddha) and are attributed accordingly as material Carnegie reproduced verbatim in the book, following the same convention used for the Dieter Rams citation in the Essentialism entry. Grouped into 5 categories mapped to the book's 4 parts plus a general 'On Human Nature and Happiness' category for standalone observations that span the whole book rather than one section. Author bio drawn from Wikipedia's Dale Carnegie entry and corroborating biographical summaries (Britannica, Missouri State Historical Society, Biography.com) for birth, education, and career facts, written as original synthesis rather than paraphrase.
